description: Language-neutral vectors for host capability resolution. Every resolver implementation -- JS, Rust, or otherwise -- runs against this file. A vector states inputs and the expected effective answer; it never states how the answer is computed.
notes: Vectors marked expectation:'current-defect' record behaviour that is WRONG TODAY and must change. They are pinned so the fix is provably a change rather than a claim. They are not desired compatibility.
Vectors marked expectation:'target' describe the contract after the resolver lands. They are expected to fail until then.
A vector's `document_kind` names which input contract it exercises: canonical | resolved_snapshot | legacy_flat.

canonical.description: Host-independent primitive contracts. Carries `adapters` only as a migration compatibility input. Must not carry effective flat `support` at primitive level.
canonical.note: predates `kind`; opened by named compatibility descriptor, never inferred

packaged_extension.description: Today's shipped packaged dictionary. Flat `support`, no `adapters`, declares its own host.
packaged_extension.note: predates `kind`; declares host, opened as legacy_flat

vectors.description: The canonical dictionary distinguishes hosts on authority-bound primitives. Support originates at provider registration, so the input supplies explicit registrations and active host state -- a bare document expecting support would restore authority to the dictionary, which the contract forbids.

DEFECT AS SHIPPED. Against the packaged dictionary the host selector changes nothing: both hosts receive byte-identical catalogs. Pinned so the fix is provable. Must NOT be read as desired compatibility.

expect_after_fix.detail: A legacy_flat document declaring host 'extension' must fail closed when projected as 'embed', not silently return extension authority.

vectors.description: The information needed to fail closed is already present and unread. Both packaged copies declare host 'extension' at primitive_dictionary.host; the bookmarklet table declares 'embed'. No code reads either. This pins both halves: the declaration exists AND it is ignored.
A formatter given an already-resolved catalog plus a disagreeing host argument fails closed. Re-selecting a host over resolved output is the shipped bug expressed as an API affordance.
An unrecognised host resolves to unsupported with a stated reason, never to a permissive default.
Validation rejects a canonical document carrying effective flat `support` at primitive level -- that shape is what makes the two input contracts confusable.
A document whose per-host detail has been flattened away must still say whose authority it encodes. Silent full-advertise is the dangerous direction.

Two hosts may legitimately produce the same effective support. That is acceptable only when the decision traces genuinely agree -- not because a selector was ignored. Both sides supply explicit provider registration, so support originates where the contract says it does.

mcp/actions-json-mcp/src/lib.rs:6812 extension_executor_supports_primitive is a hardcoded matches! over ~20 names, consulted at :6191 before the flat support check. It is extension provider-membership written inside a projection, with the host named only in the function identifier. Pinned as a defect; migrates to explicit provider registration.
support is two-valued. A leftover `partial` must fail validation rather than silently degrade to unsupported -- silent degradation is how the stale catalog rule survived unnoticed.

No active provider for the primitive's declared namespace. The user may be able to fix this by installing, configuring or activating a provider -- which is what distinguishes it from capability_unavailable and provider_unavailable, covered by the two vectors that follow.

capability_unavailable covers two sources -- a provider that never registered the primitive, and a later compatibility or context layer that narrowed it. The top-level reason is the same; the trace must say which.

The canonical dictionary declares each primitive's namespace as part of its host-independent contract, deterministically derived from the dotted prefix and validated against it. It must not declare provider instances or imply a first-party provider exists.

Two candidate providers with no explicit selection is unsupported/provider_conflict. Determinism is not consent: candidates can represent different tenants, accounts, credentials or policy scopes, so an implicit winner would silently pick an authority.

A provider or catalog selected for one authenticated principal must not authorize another. Installation alone is too coarse: one Streamlit app serves many viewer sessions, and one installation can serve many tenants.

A stale catalog CAN advertise a capability that has since been withdrawn. What makes that safe is that advertisement never confers authority and every execution boundary re-resolves current state -- not, as an earlier draft said, that a catalog can never advertise more than a call would permit. The still-valid call in the same sequence proves a moved revision alone does not wedge.

results.note: a stale observed revision must not block a still-granted call

vectors.description: A supported resolution where nothing narrowed still names a deciding layer: provider_registration, where support originated. decided_by is never null.
A settled receipt replays without executing. A rerun-based boundary redelivers the same request; executing each delivery writes twice and nothing shows it happened.
Same call_id with a different request digest fails closed. Replaying the first receipt would answer a question that was not asked.
Two concurrent deliveries of one call_id coalesce onto a single execution rather than racing.

Two viewer sessions of one app, same authenticated principal, colliding call_id by coincidence. Session 2 must execute rather than receive session 1's receipt. Changing the principal here would make this a cross-principal replay instead of an isolation case.

A call arriving under a different authenticated principal against a receipt or catalog resolved for another is not a replay and not an isolation case -- it is a cross-principal attempt, and it must reject before the handler runs. Zero handler invocations for the second call is the assertion that matters.

Restricted caller rights exist only in the container runtime. A warehouse descriptor claiming caller_rights is rejected, never downgraded -- a silent substitution changes whose privileges execute a query, invisibly.

Packaging is deployment metadata. Identical provider and authority state yields identical decisions and identical catalog fingerprints across all three projections. The parity assertions are all 'identical' claims, which a resolver that ignored host state entirely would also satisfy; differs_when_authority_differs is the control that separates real parity from a vacuous pass.
Redaction is recursive over the whole payload, not a top-level key filter. A forbidden key nested inside provider metadata reaches the browser just as readily as one at the root.
Provider active but does not register this primitive. No remediation is available to the user.
Provider registered and selected but initialization or health failed. Transient, and it must not collapse into either of the other two -- conflating them makes an outage look permanent.

vectors.ruling: #335 layer 4; coverage gap found by sabotage
vectors.description: An explicitly selected dictionary-adapters compatibility profile narrows a registered primitive. The profile makes the migration input deliberate rather than a hidden veto on every live runtime provider.

A live runtime provider that registers a primitive is authoritative for availability unless HostState explicitly selects a compatibility profile. Legacy embed metadata must not silently veto a real served-host implementation.
With a verified durable store, mutation primitives resolve normally.

vectors.description: Instance B reconstructs with a different runtime_id, which a warehouse rerun plausibly rotates. Continuity MUST survive it: a process, component instance, WebSocket, script run or reconstructed host may all rotate while viewer continuity remains valid, and keeping that volatile identity in the durable key turned every reconstruction into a silent miss. runtime_id is now diagnostics, never authority or replay identity.

A projection whose TRANSPORT is unproven exposes zero executable primitives -- reads included. I had reasoned reads were safe, which was wrong in the familiar direction: the unproven thing is the component return channel itself, not mutation durability. Snowflake proves static HTML/iframe for warehouse and does not prove an embedded agent can send a call frontend-to-Python and receive its result. A read over a transport that may not exist is as false as a mutation.

A descriptor naming a projection but omitting transport_status must not resolve supported. The previous version blocked only an explicit "proposed", so the safety property depended on every producer remembering a newly optional field -- the exact failure class this contract removes. The schema now requires the field AND the resolver fails closed on its absence, because a value reaches a resolver before any schema does.
Availability and executable schema travel together. A selected provider may add an explicitly declared parameter, and the resolved descriptor identifies that provider registration as its source.
